children.value: The chapter followed one question: how does a retrieval system built for text find images, audio, and video? Each approach bridges the semantic gap at a different level and with different costs.
Captions, alt texts, surrounding text, anchor texts
Feature vectors of colors, textures, sounds
Narrow tasks such as speech versus music
Text and media in one vector space

The approaches build on each other rather than compete. Metadata provides context that no content analysis can recover. Perceptual features describe how content looks and sounds and feed classifiers. Classifiers and generative models write metadata automatically. Shared embeddings cover the visual concepts that nobody described. Time-based media apply all of them per segment, and specialized solutions take over where a task demands exactness or robustness beyond general methods.

The semantic gap is the distance between the features a system computes from a signal and the concepts people use in queries. Text carries its meaning in its symbols; images, audio, and video do not, so their meaning must be extracted before it can be matched. Part of the gap, such as “UNESCO World Heritage Site”, cannot be closed from the content at all and needs context: metadata, the surrounding web page, or the world knowledge of a large model.
Metadata turns a multimedia search into a text search. Values are generic, specific, or abstract and are organized in facets. Standards such as EXIF, IPTC, Dublin Core, ID3, and
define where metadata is stored, not what it says. Curated catalogues such as IMDb and MusicBrainz show how well the keyword path works when someone pays for quality.

The keyword path breaks for arbitrary collections. Manual annotation costs about a dollar per item and varies in level and depth between annotators; harvested metadata from the web is cheap but can be wrong or manipulated, as Doctorow’s seven obstacles describe.

Automated content analysis climbs an abstraction ladder from raw data to perceptual, structural, semantic, and contextual representations. Perceptual feature vectors support similarity search directly or serve as input to classifiers that produce labels. They must be invariant to changes that human perception ignores, and perceptual similarity is not semantic similarity.

Neural networks replaced hand-crafted features with learned ones, from LeNet and AlexNet to ResNet and the Vision Transformer. Most of these task-specific classifiers are superseded by models trained with self-supervised and contrastive learning, whose ideas they share. Their labels are claims too: classifiers confuse similar classes, such as a coyote labeled “wolf”, and must be evaluated like human metadata.

Multimodal transformers offer two paths. The describe path generates captions, structured JSON fields, or transcripts and reuses the text toolkit, with readable but possibly hallucinated metadata. The embedding path rests on the idea that all modalities can be mapped into one embedding space. Multimodal language models use such a space inside the model, where image tokens and text tokens form one sequence; dual encoders such as CLIP give every item one vector, which enables text-to-image search and zero-shot classification without labels. Hybrid systems combine both paths.

Audio and video need retrieval units: frames, shots, scenes, and episodes for video, overlapping frames and segments for audio, in analogy to text chunking. Some tasks, such as identifying a song from a noisy phone recording, need specialized solutions like audio fingerprinting that solve one task very well and little else.
